name: The berry paradox: a banana is a berry, a strawberry isn't
strand: Foods that are secretly something surprising
scope: T1: a banana is botanically a BERRY (grows from one flower's single ovary, soft fleshy wall, tiny seeds inside; wild bananas are packed with hard seeds). T2: a strawberry is NOT a berry, the red flesh is a swollen flower base (receptacle) and the little dots on its surface are the true fruits (achenes). T2/T3: raspberries and blackberries aren't berries either, each is a cluster of tiny fruitlets from one flower with many ovaries (an aggregate fruit). T3: a tomato is a berry, and so are a grape, a kiwi, a chili pepper and an eggplant, fleshy with seeds embedded inside. T3: watermelon, cucumber and pumpkin are berries too, a hard-rind kind called a pepo. T4: an avocado is a one-seeded berry, the whole thing is fruit wall around a single giant seed. T4: the botanical test for 'berry' (one ovary, fleshy through, seeds inside) is why blueberries and grapes qualify but strawberries fail. T5: in 1893 the US Supreme Court (Nix v. Hedden) ruled the tomato a 'vegetable' for tariffs, using kitchen meaning not botany, because it's eaten with dinner not dessert.
source: Grokipedia (checked first, HTTP 403 to fetch); corroborated via Wikipedia 'Berry (botany)', 'Accessory fruit', 'Nix v. Hedden' and search summaries (Justia, Cornell LII for the 1893 ruling).
framing_note: Scene-led: lead with 'which of these is secretly a berry?', never 'What is a berry?'. Every answer is a specific food's true identity or the concrete botanical test; all four choices stay live foods. Accuracy rail: strawberry/raspberry/blackberry are NOT berries (accessory/aggregate) and the strawberry's surface dots are the real fruits, not seeds. Dinner-test payoff: the strawberry-isn't-a-berry rung. Nix v. Hedden is food-anchored (the tomato is the subject, not a bare legal fact).

name: Nuts that aren't nuts
strand: Foods that are secretly something surprising
scope: T1: a peanut is not a nut, it's a LEGUME, a cousin of peas and beans that grows in a pod. T2: the peanut plant flowers above ground, then the stalk bends down and buries the pod, so peanuts ripen UNDERGROUND (geocarpy), hence 'groundnut'. T2: an almond is not really a nut, it's the hard PIT (seed) inside a fruit like a small dry peach; almond and peach trees are close cousins (both Prunus). T3: wild/bitter almonds are POISONOUS, they carry a compound that releases cyanide; the sweet almond we eat is a rare version tamed by one flipped (recessive) gene. T3: a cashew grows as a seed hanging off the BOTTOM of a fleshy 'cashew apple', dangling outside the fruit, not tucked inside it. T3: walnuts and pecans aren't true nuts either, they're the seeds of drupes (the green husk is fruit flesh). T4: a coconut isn't a nut, it's a drupe (same fruit type as a peach), and the 'nut' is its stone. T4: the botanical true nuts are hazelnuts, chestnuts and acorns, a hard shell that doesn't split open, from one ovary. T5: peanuts can pick up a mold toxin (aflatoxin) in warm damp storage, which is why peanut crops are tested, an honest food-safety truth.
source: Grokipedia (checked first, 403); corroborated via Wikipedia 'Peanut', 'Almond', 'Cashew', 'Nut (fruit)' and search summaries (Oxford Plants 400 on Prunus dulcis; Plant Physiology on the amygdalin/bitter-almond gene).
framing_note: Scene/prep-led: 'you crack it, roast it, salt it, but it was never a nut.' Every answer names a food's real botanical identity. Accuracy rails: peanut = legume ripening underground; almond = drupe seed and a Prunus cousin of peach; label the cyanide fact honestly as the WILD/bitter almond, not the grocery-store sweet almond. Dinner-test payoff: peanuts ripen underground, or wild almonds carry cyanide. Aflatoxin is a nutrition/context truth, never tested as a lab term.

name: The poison-ivy family at your dinner table
strand: Foods that are secretly something surprising
scope: T2: cashews are never sold in their shell because the raw shell oil is CAUSTIC, it blisters skin the way poison ivy does. T3: cashews, mangoes, pistachios and poison ivy are all the SAME plant family (the cashew family, Anacardiaceae), sharing the skin-irritant oil urushiol. T3: that's why some people get an itchy rash around the mouth from mango skin, it's a mild poison-ivy reaction from a cousin plant. T4: the 'raw' cashews in stores aren't truly raw, they're steamed or roasted to destroy the shell's toxic oil, and workers who shell them by hand can get chemical burns. T4: sumac, the tangy dark-red spice in Middle Eastern cooking, comes from this same family (an edible, non-toxic sumac; poison sumac is a different cousin). T5: the cashew shell oil is so tough it's used industrially in brake linings and resins, the snack food and the machine part come from the same seed.
source: Grokipedia (checked first, 403); corroborated via Wikipedia 'Anacardiaceae', 'Urushiol', 'Cashew' and search summaries (Scientific American 'What Do Cashews, Mangoes and Poison Ivy Have in Common?').
framing_note: Matter-of-fact prep voice: 'why you never see a cashew in its shell.' Answer is always a concrete food-family fact. Accuracy rail: the culinary spice sumac is the non-toxic species and must be distinguished from poison sumac; keep 'urushiol' as context, not the tested answer (the answer is the cousin plant or the burn). Dinner-test payoff: mango and poison ivy are cousins (the mango-skin-rash rung).

name: The passion fruit and the Passion of Christ
strand: Foods that are secretly something surprising
scope: T2: passion fruit is named for the PASSION (the suffering and crucifixion) of Christ, not for romance, and 16th-century Spanish and Portuguese Jesuit missionaries in South America gave the flower its name. T3: they read the Crucifixion into the flower's parts, the frilly crown of filaments (the corona) as the crown of thorns. T3: the flower's three stigmas were read as the three nails, and the ring of anthers below as Christ's wounds. T4: the five petals and five sepals were counted as the ten faithful apostles, leaving out Peter (who denied Jesus) and Judas (who betrayed him). T4: the fruit itself is a berry on a climbing vine (a liana); in Brazil it's called maracuja and its tart pulp flavors juice, mousse and desserts.
source: Grokipedia (checked first, 403); corroborated via Kew 'A passion for passion flowers', University of Dayton Marian Library 'Passion Flower', uCatholic, and Wikipedia 'Passiflora'.
framing_note: Tell it as naming HISTORY: 'what the missionaries SAW and named', an interpretation laid onto the flower, not a claim that the flower IS a religious object. Scene-led (the flower in a missionary's hand), never 'What does the passion flower symbolize?'. Answer is a concrete part-to-reading pairing or the fruit fact. Accuracy rail: it is the Passion = suffering/Crucifixion, NOT passion = love; Jesuit missionaries, 16th c., South America. Dinner-test payoff: the corona = crown of thorns rung. Not vision-mandated: settled naming history told neutrally as interpretation, no stance taken.

name: The fig is a flower turned outside-in
strand: Foods that are secretly something surprising
scope: T2: a fig isn't a fruit in the usual sense, it's a hollow pod (a syconium) lined on the INSIDE with hundreds of tiny flowers. T3: because the flowers are sealed inside, a fig must be pollinated from within, so a tiny fig WASP crawls in through a pinhole at the bottom to do it. T3: the female wasp tears off her wings squeezing through that hole and dies inside after pollinating and laying eggs, she can't get back out. T4: the fig then makes an enzyme (ficin) that dissolves the dead wasp and absorbs her, so there is no whole insect in a ripe fig, and the crunch you feel is the fig's own seeds. T4: each fig species pairs with its OWN wasp species, an obligate partnership where neither can reproduce without the other (co-evolution). T5: most supermarket figs (like the common Black Mission) come from varieties bred to ripen WITHOUT pollination (parthenocarpic), so those figs never needed a wasp at all.
source: Grokipedia (checked first, 403); corroborated via Wikipedia 'Fig wasp', 'Ficus', 'Common fig' and search summaries (USDA Forest Service 'Fig Wasps' pollinator page).
framing_note: Scene-led wonder: 'you bite a fig, what did it once hold?' Answer is a concrete fig-biology fact. Keep the wasp matter-of-fact, never gory. Accuracy rail: ficin DISSOLVES the wasp so there is no whole insect in a ripe fig, and many commercial figs are parthenocarpic and wasp-free, do NOT overstate 'every fig contains a wasp.' Dinner-test payoff: the ficin-dissolves-the-wasp rung.

name: A pineapple is dozens of fruits fused into one
strand: Foods that are secretly something surprising
scope: T1: a pineapple is not one fruit, it's many small fruits FUSED into a single head, and each hexagonal 'eye' on the skin was once a separate flower. T2: those flowers coalesce as they ripen into a multiple fruit, which is why the surface is a mosaic of eyes instead of smooth skin. T2: a pineapple grows from the ground on a low spiky plant, it does NOT grow on a tree (a common surprise). T3: raw pineapple carries an enzyme (bromelain) that digests protein, which is why fresh pineapple stings your tongue and won't let gelatin set, it eats the gelatin's protein. T3: heat destroys that enzyme, so CANNED or cooked pineapple sets in jello while fresh pineapple doesn't. T4: a picked pineapple won't get any sweeter, it stores no starch to convert, so it must be harvested ripe, unlike a banana which keeps ripening after picking.
source: Grokipedia (checked first, 403); corroborated via Wikipedia 'Pineapple', 'Bromelain', 'Multiple fruit' and search summaries.
framing_note: Scene-led: 'count the diamonds on a pineapple's skin, each one was ___'. Answer is a concrete structure or enzyme fact; teach the CONCEPT 'a protein-digesting enzyme' and keep 'bromelain' as context, never the tested word. Accuracy rail: pineapple grows on a low ground plant, not a tree; the fresh-vs-canned jello behavior is because heat kills the enzyme. Dinner-test payoff: the 'fresh pineapple won't let jello set because it digests the protein' rung.

name: Spices are surprising parts of a plant
strand: Foods that are secretly something surprising
scope: T1: cinnamon is tree BARK, the dried inner bark of a tree, which curls into quills as it dries. T2: cloves are dried flower BUDS, picked before they bloom, each clove an unopened bud. T2: black peppercorns are dried BERRIES from a climbing vine, and green, black and white pepper are the same berry at different stages of prep. T3: saffron is the three thread-like STIGMAS from inside a single crocus flower, all hand-picked, which is why it's the world's priciest spice (invert the price hook). T3: capers are pickled unopened flower BUDS of a Mediterranean bush (a caperberry is that bush's fruit, a different thing). T3: ginger and turmeric are underground STEMS (rhizomes), not roots. T4: the 'cinnamon' in most kitchens is really CASSIA, a cheaper cousin; true Ceylon cinnamon is pale and mild, and cassia carries far more coumarin (worth knowing if you eat a lot daily). T4: vanilla, saffron and cardamom are the priciest spices, each defined by how much hand labor a tiny edible part takes. T5: paprika, cayenne and chili powder are all just dried, ground fruit of the same plant genus (Capsicum) at different heat levels.
source: Grokipedia (checked first, 403); corroborated via Wikipedia 'Cinnamon', 'Clove', 'Saffron', 'Caper', 'Black pepper' and search summaries (Healthline 'Ceylon vs Cassia').
framing_note: Scene-led, invert every price/quantity hook: 'the world's priciest spice is three threads from one flower, from what?'. Answer names the plant PART or the specific plant. Teach the concept; keep coumarin and Latin names as context/distractors only. Accuracy rail: saffron = 3 crocus stigmas per flower; most supermarket 'cinnamon' is cassia, not true Ceylon; capers = buds vs caperberries = fruit. Dinner-test payoff: the saffron = crocus stigmas rung.

name: Nutmeg and mace: one fruit, two spices, and a war
strand: Foods that are secretly something surprising
scope: T2: nutmeg and mace are TWO different spices from the SAME fruit, mace is the lacy red coat (aril) wrapped around the seed, and nutmeg is the seed inside it. T3: for centuries the nutmeg tree grew in only ONE place on earth, the tiny Banda Islands in what is now Indonesia, the original 'Spice Islands.' T3: nutmeg was once worth more by weight than gold, which drove European empires to fight over these specks of land. T4: the Dutch seized the Banda Islands in 1621 and killed or enslaved almost the entire population to lock down the world's only nutmeg supply, a brutal food-driven history. T4: in the 1667 Treaty of Breda the Dutch traded away the island of Manhattan (New Amsterdam) to Britain in order to keep the last nutmeg island, Run, nutmeg was that valuable. T5: grated nutmeg is mildly mind-altering in large doses (from myristicin), a real reason it's used only a pinch at a time.
source: Grokipedia (checked first, 403); corroborated via Wikipedia 'Nutmeg', 'Banda Islands', 'Run (island)', 'Dutch conquest of the Banda Islands' and NBC News 'Why the Banda Islands Were Once More Valuable Than Manhattan.'
framing_note: Lead with the fruit or the 'worth more than gold' hook; the FOOD (nutmeg/mace) stays the anchor even in the history rungs. Answer is a concrete spice fact or a food-driven historical beat, never a bare treaty/date. Accuracy rail: mace = aril, nutmeg = seed, same fruit; the Manhattan-for-Run swap is the 1667 Treaty of Breda; the Banda atrocity is real, state it plainly but not gorily for a kid. Dinner-test payoff: mace and nutmeg come from the same fruit (T2), or the Manhattan-for-nutmeg trade (T4).

name: Foods that are secretly made from animals
strand: Foods that are secretly something surprising
scope: T2: most cheese is set with RENNET, traditionally an enzyme from the stomach lining of a young calf, which makes milk curdle into curds and whey. T2: honey is essentially made in a bee's stomach, nectar the bee swallows, brings back up and passes mouth-to-mouth, then fans dry, and honey basically never spoils. T3: the bright red in some yogurts, candies and drinks (carmine/cochineal) is a dye made from crushed scale INSECTS that live on cactus. T3: gelatin, in gummy bears, marshmallows and jello, is collagen boiled out of animal skin and bones. T4: many clear beers and wines are fined with isinglass, made from fish swim BLADDERS, which is why some beers aren't vegetarian. T4: Worcestershire sauce and a classic Caesar dressing get their savory punch from fermented ANCHOVIES, hidden fish in the steak sauce. T5: today most cheese uses lab-grown chymosin (microbes carrying the calf gene) instead of real calf stomach, so a lot of cheese is now vegetarian, but not all.
source: Grokipedia (checked first, 403); corroborated via Wikipedia 'Rennet', 'Cochineal', 'Carmine', 'Gelatin', 'Isinglass', 'Worcestershire sauce' and Vegetarian Resource Group on microbial rennet/FPC.
framing_note: Matter-of-fact, never gross-out: 'the surprising animal source hiding in an everyday food.' Answer names the specific animal source or the food. Accuracy rail: traditional rennet = calf-stomach enzyme, but MOST modern cheese uses microbial/lab chymosin, so 'all cheese has calf stomach' is FALSE, make that correction the T5 rung; cochineal red = insect, not a plant. Dinner-test payoff: the cochineal-red-is-crushed-insects rung. Keep chymosin and carminic acid as context words, not tested answers.

name: Ketchup started out as a fish sauce
strand: Foods that are secretly something surprising
scope: T3: ketchup wasn't originally about tomatoes, the name comes from a Southeast Asian / Hokkien Chinese word (ke-tsiap) for a fermented FISH sauce (a pickled-fish brine). T3: British sailors brought the idea home and copied the dark savory sauce with local ingredients, so early English 'ketchups' were made from MUSHROOMS, walnuts, oysters or anchovies, with no tomato at all. T4: tomato ketchup was an American development, the first known tomato-ketchup recipe was published in 1812 (by James Mease). T4: early tomato ketchups spoiled fast and were loaded with preservatives; Henry Heinz's late-1800s move was to use lots of ripe tomatoes, vinegar and sugar so it kept without sketchy additives. T5: that fermented-fish ancestor is the same family as today's Southeast Asian fish sauces (nam pla, nuoc mam) and echoes ancient Rome's garum, savory umami sauces recur across history.
source: Grokipedia (checked first, 403); corroborated via Wikipedia 'Ketchup', National Geographic 'How Was Ketchup Invented?', Smithsonian Magazine, and NPR Code Switch.
framing_note: Food-driven history where the SAUCE is the anchor in every rung. Scene/origin-led. Answer is a concrete ingredient or origin fact. Accuracy rail: the word is Hokkien / Southeast Asian for a fermented-fish brine; British ketchups were mushroom/walnut/anchovy with no tomato; tomato ketchup is an early-1800s American development, do not backdate tomatoes into it. Dinner-test payoff: the 'original ketchup was fermented fish, no tomato' rung.

name: Broccoli, kale and cabbage are the same plant
strand: Foods that are secretly something surprising
scope: T1: cabbage, kale, broccoli, cauliflower, Brussels sprouts and kohlrabi are all ONE species (Brassica oleracea), the same plant bred in different directions. T2: the wild ancestor is a scrubby seaside plant (wild cabbage) that looks like leggy kale. T2: farmers made each vegetable by selecting a DIFFERENT part to swell, this is artificial selection, the same idea as breeding dogs from wolves. T3: broccoli and cauliflower are the plant's FLOWER heads harvested before they open, you're eating unopened flower buds. T3: Brussels sprouts are swollen side BUDS up the stalk, and cabbage is one giant terminal bud (a tight ball of leaves). T3: kale and collards are the LEAVES bred big and loose, while kohlrabi is the STEM bred into a swollen bulb. T4: because they're all one species they can cross-pollinate, so seed savers must keep a broccoli away from a kale to keep the seed true. T4: the mustardy bite they all share comes from the same defensive chemicals (glucosinolates) in the family, and cooking mellows it. T5: the same genus gave other crops from OTHER species, turnips, bok choy, canola and true mustard, so a big share of the vegetable aisle is close cousins.
source: Grokipedia (checked first, 403); corroborated via Wikipedia 'Brassica oleracea', Oxford Plants 400, and 'The Botanist in the Kitchen' on B. oleracea diversity.
framing_note: Scene-led: 'which of these veggies is a different species from broccoli?' (trick: none). Answer names the PLANT PART that was bred, or the shared-species fact. Accuracy rail: all listed are Brassica oleracea (broccoli/cauliflower = flower buds, sprouts/cabbage = buds, kale = leaves, kohlrabi = stem); turnip, bok choy and canola are OTHER Brassica species, do not fold them into oleracea. Dinner-test payoff: broccoli is the plant's unopened flower (T3), or 'they're all one species' (T1).

name: Chocolate is a bitter, fermented, roasted seed
strand: Foods that are secretly something surprising
scope: T1: chocolate comes from the SEEDS (beans) inside a big pod that grows straight off the trunk of the cacao tree. T2: raw cacao beans are bitter and taste nothing like chocolate, the chocolate flavor develops only after the beans FERMENT in their own fruit pulp, then are dried and roasted. T2: the white pulp around the beans in the pod is a sweet, tangy fruit you can eat, and it's the part farmers pile up to ferment. T3: white chocolate contains NO cocoa solids at all, it's made from cocoa BUTTER (the fat), sugar and milk, which is why it's pale. T3: the Aztecs and Maya drank chocolate UNSWEETENED and spiced (often with chili), a bitter frothy drink, sugar was added only after it reached Europe. T4: cocoa powder and cocoa butter are the two halves of a roasted bean pressed apart, and recombining them with sugar in different ratios is what makes dark versus milk chocolate.
source: Grokipedia (checked first, 403); corroborated via Wikipedia 'Cocoa bean', 'Chocolate', 'Theobroma cacao', 'White chocolate'.
framing_note: Origin/prep-led wonder: 'what does chocolate taste like straight off the tree?' (bitter). Answer is a concrete cacao fact. Accuracy rail: the flavor is MADE by fermentation plus roasting (beans aren't sweet raw); white chocolate has cocoa butter but no cocoa solids; Mesoamerican chocolate was an unsweetened drink, no anachronistic sugar or milk before European contact. Dinner-test payoff: white chocolate contains no cocoa solids (T3), or chocolate is fermented (T2).
